## Proof

**Indexing.** Let the matrix have size $(N+1)\times(N+1)$ with rows and columns indexed $i,j = 1,\dots,N+1$. The $(i,j)$-entry is

$$M_{ij} = \frac{b^{\,i+j-1}-a^{\,i+j-1}}{i+j-1}.$$

**Key observation.** By the fundamental theorem of calculus,

$$\frac{b^{k}-a^{k}}{k} = \int_a^b t^{k-1}\,dt, \qquad k\ge 1.$$

Setting $k = i+j-1$ gives

$$M_{ij} = \int_a^b t^{i+j-2}\,dt = \int_a^b t^{i-1}\,t^{j-1}\,dt.$$

**Gram matrix interpretation.** Define the inner product on $L^2[a,b]$:

$$\langle f, g\rangle = \int_a^b f(t)\,g(t)\,dt.$$

Then

$$M_{ij} = \big\langle t^{i-1},\; t^{j-1}\big\rangle, \qquad i,j = 1,\dots,N+1.$$

Thus $M(N+1)$ is exactly the **Gram matrix** of the monomials $\{1, t, t^2, \dots, t^N\}$ with respect to this inner product.

**Positive definiteness.** For any nonzero vector $c = (c_0, c_1, \dots, c_N)^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}$, form the polynomial $p(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} c_k t^k$. Then

$$c^T M\, c = \sum_{i,j=0}^{N} c_i\, c_j \int_a^b t^{i+j}\,dt = \int_a^b \left(\sum_{k=0}^{N} c_k t^k\right)^2 dt = \int_a^b p(t)^2\, dt.$$

Since $a \neq b$, the interval $[a,b]$ has positive length (positive Lebesgue measure). The polynomial $p$ is not identically zero (as $c \neq 0$), and a nonzero polynomial has only finitely many roots, so $p(t)^2 > 0$ on $[a,b]$ except at finitely many points. Therefore

$$c^T M\, c = \int_a^b p(t)^2\, dt > 0.$$

This holds for every nonzero $c$, so $M(N+1)$ is **positive definite**, hence invertible.

**Conclusion.** $M(N+1)$ is invertible for every positive integer $N$ and every $a \neq b$.
